question: Which statement best describes Local vs lifted vs global state?
options: State should live at the narrowest scope that works: local (useState in the one component that uses it), lifted (moved to the nearest common parent when siblings must share it), or global (Context or a store when many distant components need it). The decision rule is to start local, lift only when a sibling needs the value, and go global only when prop-drilling becomes painful. Over-globalizing creates coupling and re-renders; under-lifting causes duplicated, drifting copies.

Fetched data is not really client state — it is a cache of data owned by a server, with lifecycle concerns like staleness, revalidation, deduplication, and retries that client stores don't model. Putting server data in Redux/useState reinvents a caching layer poorly and leads to stale lists and duplicate fetches. Tools like React Query and SWR model it as server state, keying each request and refetching when it goes stale.

For shared client state, a reducer centralizes update logic while Context distributes it, forming a mini-store: dispatch actions, read state anywhere below the provider. It is built into React with no dependencies, ideal for moderate global state like theme or auth. The key limitation is that Context delivers one value and cannot slice, so a frequently-changing reducer state re-renders every consumer.

Stores like Redux and Zustand let components subscribe to a narrow slice of state via a selector, so a component only re-renders when the specific value it reads changes. This is the central re-render-avoidance technique that Context lacks — Context re-renders all consumers on any change. Selectors that return objects should use shallow equality so new-but-equal results don't trigger spurious renders.

options: The biggest performance lever in a React app is limiting which components re-render on a state change. A common misconception is that Context is a state manager you can use for everything. Context is a dependency-injection / transport mechanism: it has no built-in slicing, memoization, or selector support, so a single Context holding hot, frequently-changing state re-renders all of its consumers. Use Context for stable, low-frequency values (theme, auth, locale) and reach for a store with selectors when state changes often and consumers need only slices.

At scale the durable pattern is to layer state by kind rather than funnel everything through one store: local UI state in components, server state in React Query, genuinely global client state in a store read via selectors, and rarely-changing app values in Context. Each feature team owns its slices and query keys, keeping changes local and the re-render set minimal. Codifying these boundaries in lint rules and docs prevents the architecture from eroding as the app grows.
